sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Waiter's Carry is a single-arm overhead loaded carry that builds shoulder stability, core strength, and postural control.

The lifter holds a weight plate, dumbbell, or kettlebell overhead with one arm fully extended and walks a set distance while maintaining a tall, braced posture.

It is an excellent accessory for overhead pressing strength, scapular control, and anti-rotational core stability.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Builds shoulder stability and overhead control
- Develops anti-rotation and anti-lateral-flexion core strength
- Reinforces tall, stacked posture under load
- Improves scapular and thoracic positioning
- Highly transferable to overhead pressing
- Strengthens grip and forearm endurance
- Adjustable through load and distance

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Deltoids, Trapezius, Core (Obliques, Rectus Abdominis)

Secondary: Rotator Cuff, Triceps, Forearms, Glutes, Quadriceps

sections.heading: Set Up
sections.content:
1. Select a weight plate of appropriate load.
2. Stand next to it with your feet shoulder-width apart.
3. Squat down to pick up the plate with one hand, gripping it firmly around the edge.

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Lift the weight plate to shoulder height.
2. Carefully press it overhead until your arm is fully extended.
3. Keep your wrist straight and the plate stable above you.

sections.heading: Walk With Control
sections.content:
1. Engage your core and shoulders to maintain stability as you begin walking.
2. Keep your gaze forward and your body straight.
3. Avoid any leaning or tilting to the sides.

sections.heading: Finish the Carry
sections.content:
1. Walk a predetermined distance or for a set period of time.
2. Once completed, carefully lower the weight plate back to shoulder height and then to the ground in a controlled manner.
3. Switch arms if necessary to repeat the exercise on the other side.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Letting the carrying arm drift forward or behind the head
- Leaning to the opposite side to balance the load
- Allowing the lower back to overextend
- Holding the breath instead of breathing steadily
- Walking with rushed, choppy steps
- Bending the elbow during the carry
- Using a load too heavy to maintain alignment

sections.heading: Equipment Required
sections.content:
- Weight plate, dumbbell, or kettlebell
- Open walking space
- Optional measuring tape or distance markers

sections.heading: Body Position
sections.content:
1. Feet shoulder-width apart at the start.
2. Ribs stacked over hips, core braced.
3. Carrying arm fully locked out overhead.

sections.heading: Movement Setup
sections.content:
1. Press the load to lockout before stepping off.
2. Walk in a straight line with controlled steps.
3. Switch arms midway or at the end of the set.

sections.heading: Safety Considerations
sections.content:
- Keep the path clear of obstacles
- Stop if posture deteriorates or the arm drops
- Use a load you can press cleanly overhead
- Lower the weight with control, not by dropping it
- Stop immediately if you feel sharp shoulder or back pain
